Ways to reduce overfitting include collecting more training data, simplifying the model, regularization (L1 and L2 penalties that shrink weights; L1 can drive weights to exactly zero), early stopping, dropout for neural networks, feature selection and cross-validation to choose hyperparameters. Learning curves, which plot error against training set size, help diagnose whether a model suffers from high bias or high variance.

S4.title: Ml Lecture Notes
S4.text: 3. Generalization, Overfitting and the Bias-Variance Tradeoff A model generalizes when it performs well on new data, not just on the data used for training. Overfitting happens when a model memorizes noise and idiosyncrasies of the training set: training error is very low but validation or test error is much higher. Underfitting happens when the model is too simple to capture the pattern, so both training and validation error are high. The bias-variance tradeoff explains this. Bias is the error caused by overly simple assumptions; high-bias models underfit. Variance is the sensitivity of a model to the particular training sample; high-variance models overfit. Total expected error is bias squared plus variance plus irreducible noise. Increasing model complexity lowers bias but raises variance.

S5.title: Ml Model Diagnostics Handbook
S5.text:
3. Regularization Strength in scikit-learn
In scikit-learn LogisticRegression the parameter C is the inverse of the regularization strength: a
smaller C means stronger regularization, and the default is C=1.0. For Ridge regression the
parameter alpha works the opposite way: a larger alpha means stronger shrinkage.
L2 regularization (ridge) shrinks all weights toward zero; L1 regularization (lasso) can set some
weights exactly to zero and therefore performs feature selection.

S9.title: Ml Model Diagnostics Handbook
S9.text:
1. Reading Learning Curves
A learning curve plots training error and validation error against the training set size. In a high-bias
model both errors are high and they converge close to each other; adding more data barely helps
because the model is too simple. In a high-variance model the training error is low and a large gap
separates it from the validation error; the validation error keeps falling as more data is added, so
collecting more data helps.
When a model is overfitting the first actions to try are a simpler model, stronger regularization,
more training data or early stopping.
